I would use `reminder_draw` as a randomized encouragement instrument for county turnout, restricting identification to the 180 county-elections in the 1996–2000 pilot rather than claiming an effect for the full historical sample.
Estimate the reminder’s effects on turnout and incumbent-party vote share, respecting the election-year draw structure within the pilot states, and use their ratio to estimate the turnout effect in vote-share percentage points per turnout percentage point.
Random assignment supports independence, while the nonpartisan reminder and absence of other program changes make exclusion plausible; a local causal interpretation additionally requires monotonicity and no relevant spillovers.
The main threat is weak identification—the turnout increase is only 0.3 percentage points with a first-stage F-statistic around 4—so report the reduced form and weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets, allowing for repeated counties, even if those sets are uninformative.
I would reject `eday_rain` because the reported risk-aversion and incumbent-preference channel threatens exclusion directly, and I would not generalize the reminder-induced turnout effect beyond the pilot without additional assumptions.

Estimate the first-stage effect on turnout and the reduced-form effect on incumbent-party vote share, then use their IV ratio to estimate the percentage-point change in vote share per percentage-point increase in turnout.  
Identification requires that reminders affect vote share only through turnout and do not reduce turnout; under these assumptions, the estimate concerns reminder-induced turnout in the pilot, not necessarily turnout changes nationwide over 1948–2000.  
The main threat is weak identification—the reported first-stage F-statistic is about 4—so report weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets and the randomized reduced-form estimate, accepting potentially uninformative bounds.  
I would reject `eday_rain` as an instrument because the survey evidence indicates a possible direct weather-induced shift toward the incumbent through risk preferences, undermining exclusion despite rainfall’s effect on turnout.

I would use the randomized cash-transfer draw as an encouragement design, restricting analysis to the six pilot villages and instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with `transfer_draw` interacted with an indicator for interviews after the 1993 draw.  
Estimate the effect on reported illness episodes in the preceding four weeks using individual and survey-round fixed effects, aligning interviews with actual transfer timing and retaining the original randomized assignment.  
Identification requires that assignment affect illness only through household income, with no cross-village spillovers or assignment-related selective attrition; the fund’s lack of other interventions supports, but does not prove, exclusion.  
The main limitation is extremely weak identification—a first-stage F-statistic near 2 and only six randomized villages—so report the assignment’s intention-to-treat effect alongside weak-instrument-robust confidence sets obtained by inverting randomization tests at the village level, rather than conventional 2SLS significance tests.  
These confidence sets may be unbounded, and any income-effect interpretation is local to transfer-induced income changes rather than the full region.  
I would reject `season_rain` as an instrument because rainfall can directly affect illness through malaria, water quality, and other environmental pathways despite individual and round fixed effects.

Use `works_draw` as an instrument for rural income growth, restricting analysis to the 16 eligible districts in 1993–1995, because assignment was randomized and the documentation states that the program changed nothing else.  
Estimate the assignment effects on district-average annual riot counts and district-average income growth over those three years, then take their ratio to estimate riots per one-percentage-point increase in growth.  
Under exclusion, no spillovers, and monotonicity, this identifies a local average causal response to program-induced growth, not necessarily the effect across all 290 districts.  
The main threat is weak identification—the first-stage F-statistic is about 2 with only 16 randomized districts—so report the reduced-form effect and randomization-based Anderson–Rubin confidence sets that respect the eight-of-sixteen assignment, allowing unbounded sets rather than relying on conventional 2SLS significance.  
Reject `monsoon_dev` as an instrument because deficit monsoons increase riots even in canal-irrigated districts whose crop income is unchanged, providing evidence of a pathway outside the income channel that district and year fixed effects cannot remove.

I would use `audit_grant` as a randomized instrument for segregation, restricting the analysis to the 40 eligible cities rather than coding other cities’ missing assignments as zero.  
Use assignment to instrument segregation in 2000 and 2010, with direct general expenditure per resident in constant dollars as the outcome, year and state effects, and pre-draw spending and log population for precision.  
Random assignment supports independence, and the stated absence of any other grant effects supports exclusion; under monotonicity, the estimate identifies an instrument-induced local effect in these eligible cities, not the effect across all 2,600 cities.  
The main threat is weak identification—the first-stage F-statistic is about 2—so report the assignment’s reduced-form spending effect and weak-instrument-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets, accounting for repeated observations within cities and the lottery’s assignment mechanism.  
If those confidence sets are uninformative, conclude that this design cannot determine whether segregation lowers spending rather than interpreting an unstable two-stage least-squares estimate.  
I would not use `waterways`: its association with segregation establishes potential relevance, but waterways can directly affect infrastructure costs, flood protection, and spending needs despite state-by-year fixed effects and population controls.
